Milledgeville, the county seat, is a college town that was Georgia's capital from 1804 to 1868. Georgia College and State University and Georgia Military College fill the town with students and staff. The old Governor's Mansion and the historic district add older homes, so the housing here spans many decades.

At 267 square miles, the county runs hilly in the north and flat toward the south. Your property could be a city lot or acreage far out, and buyers for each look nothing alike.

Renting is common in Baldwin County. Only 61.1% of housing units are owner-occupied, and the middle value of an owned home is $181,900.

In 2020 the county tallied 19,988 housing units, 17.4% of them vacant. Of the occupied ones, 42.1% were rented. Between 2010 and 2020 the county lost 4.2% of its people, then gained a little, and 48.8% of residents lived in rural areas. With rentals so common, an investor may be the best fit for a tenant-occupied house you want to sell as it stands.

Visit the tax commissioner at the Baldwin County Government Building, 1601 N. Columbia Street, Suite 100, Milledgeville, GA 31061, or phone 478-445-4813. It is open weekdays from 8:30 in the morning until 4:45 in the afternoon, and closed on holidays. The county's tax site has details.

Disagree with your house's value? Ring the tax assessors at (478) 445-5300. You can pull up parcel data on qPublic. Each of the five county board members is elected from a single district, and the board helps set the county's portion of the millage rate. The school board adds its own rate.

  • Tax commissioner: what you owe, payments, liens, closing statements
  • Tax assessors: your value, returns, exemptions, appeals
  • Clerk of Superior Court: recorded deeds and liens

Most bills come due November 15 after going out at least 60 days earlier. Some carry December 15 instead. Whatever date is printed on your bill is the one to follow, and the commissioner can clear up any doubt.

Paying in two parts is allowed, though the unpaid remainder keeps accruing. A check sent by mail is on time when its postmark is no later than the deadline. If the deadline lands on a weekend or holiday, you get the next business day. Out front there is a drop box. Paying by card brings a processor fee of 2.57% (3% for American Express), minimum $1.50.

  • Monthly interest runs at prime plus 3 points
  • Penalties start at 5% once 120 days pass, add another 5% every 120 days, and stop when they total 20%
  • No penalty for homesteaded property when the bill is under $500
  • Mobile homes: April 1 due date, 10% penalty, and a possible State Court citation

Ask the tax commissioner for a payoff in writing. The closing agent then deducts that amount from what you receive. In Georgia the year's tax follows the January 1 owner. The office records a lien under that owner's name unless Suite 100 gets a closing statement that shows the buyer took over the bill, and it must arrive within 90 days after the due date.

A bill that still reaches you after closing should go on to the buyer, with a settlement statement copy sent to the office. An unpaid bill can lead to a FiFa lien on the General Execution Docket at the Clerk of Superior Court, and the county says such an entry can stay on credit files for seven years or longer.

Insist on a dated payoff. Interest accrues monthly but delinquent notices rarely go out that often, so last week's figure can come up short. Rentals, inherited houses and vacant ones may owe for several years, so request the history for each year you held the property.

Step by step, a clean sale usually looks like this:

  1. Bring your deed or parcel number and any bills you still have to Suite 100.
  2. Get the payoff in writing, with the date it is good through.
  3. Hand the closing agent that figure.
  4. Return the signed closing statement to the office within 90 days of the due date.

A cash buyer who takes the house as-is can close fast, which helps when a penalty date is near. The tax still gets paid at closing, but you avoid repair requests and lender delays.

The clock runs 45 days from the date on your assessment notice. Submit a written appeal to the Board of Tax Assessors on the state form and pick a ground from four: taxability, value, uniformity or a denied exemption.

The filing also chooses your route. Take the Board of Equalization path and the assessors may amend the value first, after which you have 30 days to contest the amended notice. If that fails, a hearing is set, and Superior Court is the step beyond it. Only non-homestead real property valued at $1,000,000 or more can go to a hearing officer, who has to be a certified appraiser. Arbitration calls for a certified appraisal, and its result is final.

Before filing, open your parcel on qPublic and compare it with nearby houses. Collect photos of damage, a repair estimate or a recent appraisal, and keep copies of whatever you submit. A lower value saves money only while you own the house, but an appeal still pending can give a buyer something to discuss.

State revenue staff have no power to overrule the assessors, a board, a hearing officer, an arbitrator or a court on one parcel. For a mobile home the clock is 45 days from the bill's mailing or from April 1, whichever comes last.

Homestead relief here comes from two layers, the state's and Baldwin County's own, and you get whichever is bigger. Your application has to reach the assessors by April 1 in the first year. After approval it renews by itself.

  • Be the owner and the resident on January 1 of that first year
  • A second homestead claim anywhere, in Georgia or out of state, is barred
  • Owners aged 62 and up with household income at or under $15,000 may defer the tax
  • Farmland that qualifies is assessed at 30%, not 40%, and current-use programs tie you to a 10 or 15 year covenant

Timing matters. A buyer who closes after the April 1 cutoff will generally have to wait until the next year to benefit. Tell the buyer's agent whether a homestead exemption is on the property now, because the new owner has to apply separately.

Call (478) 445-5300 for today's amounts, and bring proof of age, income or service if your exemption depends on it.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Baldwin County tax bill?
faqs.a: The tax commissioner answers at 478-445-4813. Walk-ins go to Suite 100 at 1601 N. Columbia Street in Milledgeville.

faqs.q: Can I pay online in Baldwin County?
faqs.a: Yes. The county runs an online payment page and charges a processor fee on cards. Paying in person, by mail or in the drop box works too.

faqs.q: Does a sale wipe out the bill for that year?
faqs.a: No. The January 1 owner stays on record for that year, and only a closing statement delivered within 90 days of the due date changes who a lien names.

faqs.q: What fraction of value is taxed in Baldwin County?
faqs.a: Forty percent of market value, or 30% when the land qualifies as agricultural. Exemptions are deducted first, and then the millage rate is applied.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to contest a Baldwin County value?
faqs.a: Forty-five days, starting on the date of the notice. Mobile homes follow a different start: the bill's mailing or April 1, whichever falls later.
